3
What are the SI base units of the watt?
A
J s–1
B
kg m2
s–3
C
kg m2
s–1
D
N m s–1

hints: Start from what the watt measures: power as work done per time, $P = W/t$, so $1 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ J s}^{-1}$.
Break the joule into base units by using $W = Fs$ and $F = ma$, so $1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N m}$ and $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2}$.
Combine the $\text{kg}$, $\text{m}$ and $\text{s}$ powers from $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$ times $\text{m}$ divided by $\text{s}$, and check the final power of $\text{s}$ carefully.
walkthrough: Identify the watt as the unit of power: $1 \text{ W} = 1 \text{ J s}^{-1}$ because power is energy transferred per unit time.
Express the joule using work: $1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N m}$ because work done is force times distance moved.
Express the newton in SI base units using $F = ma$: $1 \text{ N} = 1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2}$.
Substitute back: $1 \text{ W} = (1 \text{ kg m s}^{-2})(1 \text{ m})(1 \text{ s}^{-1})$.
Combine powers: $\text{kg}$ to power 1, $\text{m}^{1+1} = \text{m}^{2}$, and $\text{s}^{-2-1} = \text{s}^{-3}$, giving $\text{kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-3}$.
This uses only the base units kilogram, metre and second. This is option B.

A.explanation: This is $\text{J s}^{-1}$, which is correct for power but $\text{J}$ is a derived unit, not an SI base unit.

B.explanation: Power as energy per time reduces to $\text{kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-3}$, which uses only SI base units.

C.explanation: This has $\text{s}^{-1}$ instead of $\text{s}^{-3}$, which corresponds to energy in base units, not power.

D.explanation: This is $\text{N m s}^{-1}$, which still contains the newton, a derived unit, not only base units.
